eyebrow: Step 1 — each plan item becomes a function
caption: clean_orders chains every small function in order with .pipe().

code:
iso = pd.to_datetime(out["order_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
us = pd.to_datetime(out["order_date"], format="%m/%d/%Y", errors="coerce")
out["order_date"] = iso.fillna(us)
caption: Parse with each format, failures become NaT, then fillna combines the two results — every date matches one format.
Three tests in all — date/price parsing, the quantity filter, and real-file checks. All passed.

eyebrow: Step 3 — run it and track the funnel
code:
raw = pd.read_csv("data/raw/orders_raw.csv")
clean = clean_orders(raw)
print(len(raw), len(raw.drop_duplicates()), len(clean))
# 1530 -> 1500 -> 1442
caption: Always report how many rows cleaning removed — losing ~4% to the quantity rule deserves a sentence.

eyebrow: Step 4 — where and when does revenue come from?
code:
sales = clean[clean["status"] == "complete"]   # 1,267 orders
sales["revenue"].sum()                           # ~$183,979
sales.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
monthly = sales.groupby("month")["revenue"].sum()
caption: North leads regions (~$50,958); Electronics leads categories despite fewer orders, at a $346 average.

code:
orders["discount_band"] = pd.cut(orders["discount_pct"],
    bins=[-1, 0, 10, 20, 30], labels=["0%","1-10%","11-20%","21-30%"])
orders.groupby("discount_band").agg(
    avg_quantity=("quantity","mean"),
    return_rate=("status", lambda s: (s=="returned").mean()))
# avg qty flat ~3.0 / return rate climbs 7.2% -> 12.6%
caption: Discounts didn't raise items per order; returns ran higher in discounted bands — a lead, not proof (103 orders in the top band).
